hook: Claude Shannon studied electrical engineering and mathematics at the University of Michigan before arriving at MIT, where his 1937 master's thesis showed that Boolean algebra could be used to design and simplify electrical switching circuits, groundwork that digital computer design would later depend on. He earned a PhD in mathematics from MIT in 1940 and spent the years after at Bell Telephone Laboratories, where during the Second World War he worked on fire-control systems and cryptography, producing a classified analysis of secrecy systems that he published openly after the war. In 1948 he published A Mathematical Theory of Communication in the Bell System Technical Journal, defining information mathematically in terms of entropy and showing how much data could reliably be sent over a noisy channel, work that founded information theory and underlies how modern computing represents and transmits information. He returned to MIT as a professor in 1956, continuing his research in communication theory while also experimenting with early electromechanical devices, including a maze-solving device called Theseus that used simple relays to learn a path, an early demonstration of machine memory and adaptive behavior. His concepts of the bit, entropy and channel capacity gave computing a rigorous vocabulary for measuring and manipulating information, an influence that reaches into how artificial intelligence systems handle information and uncertainty. He died in 2001 after some years of declining health.
